summary: Describes requirements for IPng candidates with respect to military tactical radio frequency communication networks. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A paper explaining what soldiers' radio networks need from the next Internet design.

subtitle: Requirements for military radio networks to support the next Internet Protocol

tldr.problem: Military tactical radio frequency networks have unique requirements that may not be met by standard Internet protocols. These include support for security, mobility, multicast, quality of service, and efficient operation over low-bandwidth RF links.
tldr.mechanism: This document identifies and explains the critical requirements that IPng candidates must address to support military tactical RF communication networks, including needs for compact headers, priority-based routing, and resource reservation.
tldr.outcome: IPng designers can use these requirements as criteria for evaluating protocol candidates for military deployment. The document emphasizes that compact protocol headers are essential for efficient data transfer on low-throughput RF systems.

today: RFC 1677 is an Informational document that provides context for IPng requirements from the military tactical RF community. It has not been obsoleted and remains a reference for understanding the needs of military communication networks.

sections.title: Introduction and Context
sections.content:
This RFC describes requirements for Internet Protocol next generation (IPng) when applied to military tactical radio frequency (RF) communication networks. The document is based on experiences from NATO interoperability projects and U.S. Navy initiatives exploring how commercial Internet technology can serve military tactical RF networks.

The goal is to ensure that IPng candidates can meet the special demands of military communication: supporting large numbers of local devices on individual platforms while maintaining global connectivity, operating efficiently on low-capacity RF systems, and handling the dynamic, mobile nature of tactical networks.
sections.eli5: The U.S. Navy and NATO are trying to use regular Internet technology on soldier radio networks, but those networks are different from normal Internet links. This paper explains what features the next Internet needs to work on military radios.

sections.title: Key Requirements for Tactical RF Networks
sections.content:
Scaling and addressing: While supporting 10^12 nodes is adequate, efficient address assignment is more important. Military platforms may have many local devices that do not need global addresses, suggesting a need for hierarchical or flexible addressing that distinguishes globally-unique from locally-unique addresses.

Security: Information security and authentication are paramount. Network layer security mechanisms are needed for routing authentication, source authentication, and user access control. However, in many tactical environments, link layer security already provides protection, so IPng should allow efficient operation without network layer overhead when not needed.

Mobility: Tactical systems are inherently mobile. Platforms may move in and out of RF line-of-sight, switching between different RF media (UHF, HF, satellite). Additionally, entire subnetworks such as Navy ships or aircraft strike forces move together. IPng must support both node mobility and subnet mobility.
sections.eli5: Soldiers need Internet addresses that work on their platforms, strong security to prevent enemies from reading or forging messages, and support for moving around while staying connected.

sections.title: Flows, Resource Reservation, and Quality of Service
sections.content:
Tactical RF networks have extremely limited capacity shared among multiple users and applications. Resource reservation is critical to control access and ensure quality-of-service delivery for multimedia communication.

The RFC describes experience with CSNI projects where simple QoS metrics were insufficient. Voice calls could not be routed based on a single parameter (delay, capacity, or cost); instead, a more complex reservation protocol was needed that combined multiple QoS metrics. A Flow Identification field in IPng could help map datagram services to specialized subnetwork services and allow routers to identify packets requiring special delivery requirements, particularly when those packets are encrypted.

Multicast is essential in tactical environments because the broadcast nature of RF media and the need for rapid dissemination of information make multicast the general case for information flow, not the exception.
sections.eli5: Military radios have very limited bandwidth that many people share. The Internet needs to support marking messages as important (like a missile trajectory alert) so they get through first, and letting many people receive the same message efficiently.

sections.title: Deployment, Transition, and Media Diversity
sections.content:
The transition timeline for deploying IPng in military systems is constrained. A rapid selection of IPng is important to avoid multiple transition phases: first from proprietary systems to IP, then from IP to IPng. The Department of Defense already has substantial IP deployments, making the IP-to-IPng transition a significant issue.

Tactical communication environments use a broad spectrum of media from fiber-optic LANs to very low data rate RF links below 2400 bits per second. Many RF links exhibit error statistics not well-served by higher-layer reliable protocols like TCP, so efficient lower-layer protocols may provide reliable datagram delivery at the link layer.

RF communication must not be viewed as simple point-to-point links; complex subnetwork protocols are often used to meet survivability, performance, and anti-jamming requirements. IPng will often share layer 3 duties with other protocols. Header compression mechanisms are highly valuable for maximizing throughput on limited RF bandwidth.
sections.eli5: The military is deploying Internet technology on old radio equipment, so the transition to new protocols needs to happen quickly. Radios range from very fast fiber links to slow radio channels, and messages might need to work even if radio noise corrupts bits.

sections.title: Datagram Service and Survivability
sections.content:
The connectionless datagram service paradigm provides important benefits for tactical networks. The inherent statefulness of datagram headers provides survivability in dynamic tactical environments where routers and relay points are never 100 percent available.

The efficiency with which multicast can be implemented in a connectionless network is critical when rapid information dissemination can decide the outcome of military operations. Datagram services have proven capable of supporting connection-oriented and real-time communication services in several Internet applications.

IPng should consider coexisting with circuit-switching architectures that offer demand-based control over topology and connectivity, such as the dial-up IP routing approach used for RF networks that can be dynamically allocated based on operational needs.
sections.eli5: The datagram method (sending independent messages rather than maintaining a connection) works better for military radios because routers can disappear unexpectedly, and you need to send the same message to many people at once.

references.text: Carpenter, B., and Y. Rekhter, "Internet Protocol, Next Generation (IPng): A White Paper on Transition and Other Considerations", RFC 1550, May 1994.
